teaser.text: Texas Instruments sells the chips and calculators that make electronic equipment use electricity, sense the world and follow instructions. Its business is a loop: engineers choose its parts, factories make and stock them, customers buy them for equipment, and TI keeps what remains after the costs of making and supporting them.

blocks.heading: Where could TI's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The forecast points to moderate weighted upside, but a wide distribution of outcomes. The probability-weighted price reaches $300.86 in October 2027, including dividends, for a 9% return from today’s $280.56. It rises to $336.72 in October 2028, a 24% return, and $372.93 in October 2029, a 40% return.
By October 2029, the bear case gives $154.60, while the bull case gives $624.53. The probabilities are 25% bear, 55% base and 20% bull, so the central recovery is more likely than either extreme.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for TI, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The base assumes recovery from the $9,458 million trailing proxy. Q2 2026 revenue grew 23% year over year, while Analog grew 26% and Embedded Processing grew 16%. The bear case assumes weaker demand and underused factories. The bull case requires broad orders, stronger loading and earned Silicon Labs savings.

blocks.heading: How much cash does TI really make?

paragraphs.text: Profit is an accounting result; free cash flow is what remains after investment. TI generated $7,153 million from operations in 2025. Capital spending was $4,550 million, leaving ordinary free cash flow of $2,603 million.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for TI today?

paragraphs.text: The trailing P/E, or price-to-earnings ratio, compares the share price with earnings per share from the past year. The forward P/E uses estimated earnings for the next year. TI’s 42.7x trailing P/E implies earnings of about $6.57 per share, while its 27.3x forward P/E implies about $10.28. The price has not changed; the expected earnings denominator has. Like judging a restaurant while it is temporarily closed, the valuation looks reasonable only if customers return.

dividend.title: TI dividend: payout, cash coverage and yield
dividend.meta_description: TI's dividend payout, cash coverage, forecast changes and current yield, explained in plain English.
dividend.opening: TI’s forecast dividend starts at $6.08 per share, after TI raised its quarterly payment to $1.52, and rises to $6.38 and $6.70 in the base case. In 2025, TI paid $4,999 million in dividends against $2,603 million of free cash flow, so cash did not cover the payout.
dividend.closing: The full memo also examines TI’s business, rivals, management decisions and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does TI pay per share?

paragraphs.text: Dividends begin at $6.08 per share because TI raised its quarterly payment to $1.52. The base case grows the payout to $6.38 and then $6.70. The bear case freezes it before cutting to $5.50, while the bull case reaches $7.49. The base is below the recent growth rate because 2025 shareholder payments exceeded ordinary free cash flow.

blocks.heading: Does TI’s dividend stay covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Shareholder payments exceeded the remainder. In 2025, dividends of $4,999 million and buybacks of $1,477 million totalled $6,476 million. TI therefore paid out more than its free cash flow, using reserves, investment sales and borrowing to cover the difference.

blocks.heading: What is TI’s dividend yield against its share price?

paragraphs.text: At $280.565 a share, TI’s market value is $256,225 million. Market value is what investors collectively assign to the shares. When one investor buys a share, the money normally goes to the investor selling it, not to TI.

The 2.0% dividend yield offers cash to shareholders, while the 1.0% free-cash-flow yield measures cash left after capital spending. The dividend can exceed one year’s free cash flow during a factory investment cycle. The planned Silicon Labs acquisition adds another claim on future cash, because TI will fund the approximately $7.5 billion enterprise value with cash and borrowing.

earnings.title: TI earnings: guidance and what to watch
earnings.meta_description: TI reports on October 21, 2026; watch whether demand becomes recurring cash.
earnings.opening: TI's next results are expected on October 21, 2026. Watch whether demand becomes recurring cash.
earnings.closing: The full memo answers how TI makes money, who its rivals are, how management is run and paid, and what risks could disrupt its recovery.

paragraphs.text: Texas Instruments offers moderate upside if demand recovers, factories load and investment converts into durable cash. For the quarter to September 2026, management guided on July 22 to revenue of $5,650–$6,150 million. It guided to EPS of $2.23–$2.57. For 2026, TI guided capital expenditures of $2–$3 billion. It also guided free cash flow per share of at least $8.00.

blocks.heading: What has TI's revenue and profit trend been?

paragraphs.text: The quarterly evidence is more encouraging. Revenue rose from $4,151 million in September 2024 to $4,742 million in September 2025, then reached $5,463 million in June 2026. In the second quarter of 2026, Analog revenue grew 26% and Embedded Processing revenue grew 16%. That difference shows where demand is strongest.

Consolidated gross margin reached 61.4% and operating margin 42.3%. Silicon Labs transaction costs reduced operating profit by $17 million, a small charge beside the underlying improvement. Net income reached $1,980 million, while diluted EPS rose to $2.14. Discrete tax benefits helped those results, so the underlying improvement was somewhat smaller.

The October 21, 2026 results call will test third-quarter guidance and provide the next outlook. Investors should listen for broad industrial and automotive demand, any meaningful contribution from pricing, and whether higher production becomes customer shipments or unsold inventory. Factory loadings matter because fuller plants spread fixed costs across more chips.

The key takeaway is simple: an earnings beat is not enough. TI must convert orders into recurring cash, use incentives without depending on them, and fund Silicon Labs without weakening the dividends and factories that define what comes next.
